stories.headline: Hundreds of thousands still without power after Thanksgiving storm on the East Coast
stories.summary: A storm brought heavy rain and high winds to the East Coast from Virginia to New York on Thanksgiving, downing trees and power lines, flooding roads and rail lines and prompting water rescues. Skies cleared Friday and utilities were restoring service, but roughly 400,000 to 490,000 customers were still without power on Friday, according to outlet tallies.
stories.why_it_matters: If you live in the affected states, power may still be out and travel may be slow through the holiday weekend; some families postponed Thanksgiving dinners.
stories.background: The storm hit on Thanksgiving Day, one of the busiest travel periods of the year. Severe weather also hit the West Coast and parts of the Midwest over the holiday. Outages were heaviest in the Northeast, with New Jersey and Pennsylvania among the hardest-hit states. In New York City, wind forced Macy's to postpone its Thanksgiving Day Parade to Saturday.

NewsNation reported that outages peaked at about 940,000 customers on Thanksgiving.
Bloomberg and The New York Times put the number still without power on the East Coast at more than 400,000.
The storm uprooted trees in Queens and Manhattan and flooded commuter rail lines in New Jersey, according to Bloomberg.
Pennsylvania and neighboring states were still badly affected on Friday, the BBC reported.
Some Americans canceled or moved Thanksgiving dinners to later days because of outages, The New York Times reported.

stories.headline: EPA says early tests show little lead contamination after Army detonation in Iowa
stories.summary: The EPA said its first soil and water samples, taken after the Army's controlled detonation of degraded lead azide in Iowa on Wednesday, showed negligible contamination, and that no airborne lead had been detected. stories.background: Lead azide is an explosive used in detonators. The Army said a stockpile at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant near Burlington had degraded to the point where it could explode on its own, and the EPA issued an emergency permit for a controlled detonation. stories.headline: U.S. disables another ship trying to run its blockade of Iran
stories.summary: A U.S. military aircraft fired on the Palau-flagged M/V Pacific Archer in the Gulf of Oman on Thursday and disabled its propulsion after it tried to breach the U.S. naval blockade of Iranian ports, U.S. Central Command said. An adviser to Iran's supreme leader said Tehran would neither reopen the Strait of Hormuz nor allow the blockade to stand. Separately, Kuwait summoned Iran's ambassador after a drone strike killed two Italian technicians.
stories.why_it_matters: The standoff around the Strait of Hormuz, a key route for the world's oil, keeps pressure on fuel and shipping costs, and each confrontation raises the chance of a wider fight that could draw in more countries.
stories.background: The United States has been in an armed conflict with Iran in 2026 and has enforced a naval blockade of Iranian ports, first from April to June and again since July, after a short-lived deal broke down. U.S. forces have repeatedly fired on commercial ships that ignored orders to turn back. Iran, in turn, has kept the Strait of Hormuz closed to much traffic. President Trump has used the blockade to squeeze Iran's economy while diplomatic talks have stalled.

stories.headline: Canada's Supreme Court largely upholds Quebec's religious-symbols ban
stories.summary: Canada's Supreme Court on Friday upheld most of Quebec's Bill 21, which bars teachers, police officers and other public employees in positions of authority from wearing religious symbols at work. The court affirmed Quebec's use of the constitution's override clause to shield the law, while leaving room for future legal scrutiny, according to The New York Times. Muslim and civil-rights groups called the ruling a setback.
stories.why_it_matters: Public workers in Quebec who wear a hijab, turban, kippah or cross can still be barred from many government jobs, and the ruling shapes how far Canadian provinces can override constitutional rights.
stories.background: Quebec passed Bill 21 in 2019, saying it protects the province's secular character; it was the first law of its kind in North America. To shield it from court challenges, the province invoked Section 33 of Canada's Charter of Rights, the so-called notwithstanding clause, which lets legislatures override some rights for five years at a time. A lower court struck down parts of the law in 2021, but Quebec's appeal court restored it in 2024. The Supreme Court heard the combined appeals in a four-day hearing earlier in 2026, with the federal government asking it to set limits on the override power.

facts.text: The Supreme Court upheld most of the Quebec law banning public employees in positions of authority, including teachers and police officers, from wearing religious symbols at work.
The court affirmed Quebec's use of a constitutional power to override certain rights.
The 2019 law covers symbols including Muslim headscarves, Sikh turbans, Jewish skullcaps and Christian crosses.
The National Council of Canadian Muslims called the ruling a 'significant setback' for rights.
Rights groups warned the ruling unfairly targets Muslim women; the South China Morning Post called it a political win for Quebec's sovereigntist government.
The federal government had argued before the court that the override clause does not fully shield laws from judicial review.

stories.headline: Explosion near a school in eastern Afghanistan kills at least 7 students
stories.summary: An explosion struck a middle school in Afghanistan's Kunar province on Saturday morning, killing at least seven people and wounding more than 90, according to officials. stories.background: Afghanistan has been ruled by the Taliban since 2021, and its interior ministry is the main source of official information about incidents like this. Kunar is a mountainous province on the border with Pakistan, and its capital is Asadabad. The country has large mineral deposits, and mining using explosives has expanded in recent years. Blasts from old ordnance and mining explosives are a recurring hazard for civilians there.

stories.headline: Zelenskyy questions Trump calling Putin a 'friend' as an EU loan for Ukraine stalls
stories.summary: In a BBC interview in Kyiv, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called President Trump's description of Vladimir Putin as 'my friend' strange and likened it to calling Adolf Hitler a friend during World War II. Separately, EU leaders failed to agree on the bloc's 2028-2034 budget, leaving a planned loan to Ukraine in limbo; they will try again in three weeks.

stories.background: Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. President Trump has pushed for a negotiated end to the war and has spoken warmly of Putin at times, while Zelenskyy has pressed Washington to toughen its stance on Moscow. The European Union has become Ukraine's main financial backer and has been negotiating a large loan to Kyiv. That loan is now tied up in talks over the EU's next long-term budget, which all member states must approve.

stories.summary: Spaniards vote Sunday in a snap general election that polls suggest could end Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez's eight years in power. Mamdani said during his campaign that he would follow the Council's closure plan, and since taking office he has opened a jail unit at Bellevue Hospital and named Dana Kaplan as the city's Close Rikers official. stories.headline: Mamdani has surgery for torn Achilles tendon after soccer injury
stories.summary: Mayor Zohran Mamdani had surgery on Friday to repair his right Achilles tendon, which he tore in a soccer match against local journalists. His press secretary said the surgery was successful and that he is recovering at Gracie Mansion and expected to make a full recovery.
stories.why_it_matters: City Hall says the mayor plans to be back at work Monday, so city business should continue largely as normal, but he will miss weekend public events, including the rescheduled parade.
stories.background: Mamdani, a Democrat, took office as mayor in January 2026. He was hurt earlier this month in a recreational soccer game between City Hall and members of the press, and appeared on Thanksgiving Day at an event in Harlem visibly hobbled. A torn Achilles tendon usually requires surgery and a recovery of several months.

stories.headline: Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade, postponed by the storm, steps off on Saturday
stories.summary: Macy's postponed its 100th Thanksgiving Day Parade from Thursday to Saturday morning because of forecast high winds and heavy rain, the first weather postponement in the event's history. The rescheduled parade is set for 8:30 a.m. today, and the delay forced tourists, bands and performers to rework their travel plans.
stories.why_it_matters: Expect Saturday morning street closures along the Upper West Side and Midtown parade route, crowds around Herald Square, and transit crowding near the route.
stories.background: The Macy's parade has run in Manhattan since 1924 and this year marks its 100th edition. City rules adopted after a 1997 balloon accident injured a spectator limit balloon flights in strong winds. Before this year the parade had been called off only during World War II, from 1942 to 1944, because of helium and rubber shortages. A nor'easter forecast for Thanksgiving Day brought gusts that Macy's said made the balloons unsafe.

facts.text: Macy's announced on Wednesday, Nov. 25, that the parade would move to Saturday at 8:30 a.m.
The Thanksgiving morning forecast called for sustained winds around 20 to 22 mph, gusts up to 40 mph and heavy rain.
It is the first time the parade has been postponed because of weather.
A second public balloon-inflation viewing on Friday was canceled, the parade's producer said.
Some out-of-town marching bands had to extend their stays or change plans to take part in the rescheduled parade.

stories.headline: Body recovered from Jeep swept into water off Staten Island as nor'easter outages linger
stories.summary: A body was recovered from a Jeep that went into the water off Staten Island during the Thanksgiving Day storm, the Daily News reported. The nor'easter flooded low-lying streets in several boroughs, and more than 500,000 homes along the East Coast were still without power Friday morning.
stories.why_it_matters: Coastal and low-lying neighborhoods on Staten Island, in southern Brooklyn and in Queens took the worst flooding, and the death is a reminder of the danger of driving through flooded roads.
stories.background: A strong coastal storm, or nor'easter, moved up the East Coast on Thanksgiving Day, Nov. 26, bringing heavy rain and high winds. In New York City it caused street flooding, closed some coastal roads and led Macy's to postpone its parade. Power outages stretched from North Carolina to Connecticut, with Pennsylvania, New Jersey and Maryland among the hardest hit on Friday.

facts.text: A body was recovered from a Jeep that was pulled into the waters off Staten Island during the Thanksgiving storm.
More than 500,000 homes from North Carolina to Connecticut were without power on Friday morning.

stories.headline: Mamdani and Amazon spar on Black Friday over City Council delivery-worker bill
stories.summary: Mayor Mamdani used Black Friday to urge the City Council to pass the Delivery Protection Act, a bill that would require companies such as Amazon to directly employ the drivers at their local delivery hubs instead of using subcontractors. Amazon pushed back, warning that the bill could raise customers' fees, and Fox Business reported that 150,000 customers had contacted the Council in opposition.
stories.why_it_matters: The bill could change how packages are delivered in the city and what workers and customers get out of it, and a Council vote could come by the end of the year. In today's ingest only right-leaning outlets, Fox Business and the New York Post, covered the Black Friday exchange.
stories.background: Council Member Tiffany Cabán introduced the bill, Intro 518, earlier this year, and it had a committee hearing in April. Amazon delivers most packages in the city through 'delivery service partners,' small firms that employ the drivers; the bill would make large last-mile operators employ those drivers directly and get a city license for their facilities. Mamdani announced his support in August. Amazon has argued the change would mean slower and costlier deliveries, while unions and supporters say subcontracting lets the company avoid responsibility for drivers' working conditions.

facts.text: The bill would require operators of certain last-mile delivery facilities to directly employ their delivery workers rather than rely on subcontracted delivery partners, and to be licensed by the city.
Mamdani announced his support for the bill in August.
On Black Friday, Mamdani called on the Council to pass the bill.
Amazon has warned that the bill could raise fees on New Yorkers' orders.

markets.summary: U.S. stocks rose in Friday's shortened post-Thanksgiving session, capping what the Associated Press called Wall Street's best week in more than a year. Tech shares led: the Nasdaq gained 2.3% Friday as investors bought back into AI stocks after Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia's chief executive, though the index is still down about 9% over the past month. Overseas, Chinese shares jumped after Beijing pledged to support its markets, and Japan's Nikkei also rose about 2%. Gold and other precious metals rebounded as appetite for risk returned, while bitcoin slipped and remains down about a quarter over the month. Treasury yields edged lower, and the 30-year mortgage rate sits at 7.21%.

movers.why: The tech-heavy index jumped 2.3% Friday to finish its best week in months, as investors returned to AI and chip stocks after Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia, though it remains about 9% below its level a month ago.

movers.why: The Dow rose 1.2% in the holiday-shortened session as the rebound spread beyond tech, putting it above 50,700.

movers.name: Bitcoin
movers.why: Bitcoin fell 1.2% to about $59,900 and did not join the stock rally; it is down about 26% over the past month, and no single cause stands out.

concept.explanation: A relief rally is a sharp rise in prices after a selloff, driven less by new good news than by the easing of a specific fear. This week's jump in tech stocks after Nvidia brought back Jensen Huang is an example: investors who had sold on worries about the company's leadership bought back in once that worry faded. Relief rallies can be short-lived if the deeper concerns, such as doubts about AI spending, remain, so analysts watch whether gains hold over the following weeks. They matter to your wallet because index funds in 401(k)s and IRAs rise and fall with these swings, and a quick bounce does not always mean a downturn is over.
